title: My agent runs on the exact loop architecture Claude Code's creator just described
body:
A few weeks ago Boris Cherny, who built Claude Code, posted something that got 1.26 million impressions: "I don't prompt Claude anymore. Loops prompt Claude for him." He laid out a template. One goal-spec prompt. A file called LOOP-STATE.md that remembers what got done across runs. A hard rule that nothing counts as done until it is proven with evidence. A "needs me" list where the human-only decisions get parked.

I run an agent named Arc that has operated exactly that way for months, before this had a name. So I asked Arc to read Cherny's post, plus two related ones describing the same shift from different seats, and check its own code line by line against every claim. Not summarize the vibe. Point at the actual file and line where each piece already exists.

Arc came back with a table. The sensor cadence Cherny calls Tier 1 loops is a function called claimSensorRun in Arc's own sensor code, at skills/agent-health/sensor.ts:686, the exact line where Arc's own health check starts itself. The nightly cloud routines he calls Tier 2 are Arc's dispatch loop, running lock-gated against fresh git worktrees. The swarm-of-agents Tier 3 is a fan-out pattern Arc already has wired up, each branch isolated, changes discarded if they fail validation instead of touching the main tree. LOOP-STATE.md, the durable memory file, is Arc's MEMORY.md, read at the start of every single work cycle for over a year now.

Here is the part I did not expect, and the part I trust more than the flattering comparison. Arc did not stop at "look, I already do this." It told me where the comparison breaks. Cherny's loop pings him the second something surprising happens mid-task and treats his reply as the next thing the loop runs on. Arc has no version of that. It can tell me a task finished, or failed, or got blocked, but it cannot interrupt itself mid-task to ask a question and then pick back up with my answer. It just told me plainly: that gap is real, and closing it means building a channel that has to be as carefully guarded against bad input as everything else Arc reads, because a channel that lets me interrupt Arc is a channel something else could try to abuse too.

It also flagged that its own definition of "done" is judgment, not a score. The Cursor engineer in the same batch of posts, Eric Zakariasson, says his whole method starts with locking a definition of done the agent can grade against a metric or test suite. Arc's tasks do not carry anything like that. Arc has thousands of completed tasks behind a track record that has held up, but it told me directly that a track record is not the same claim as a structural guarantee, and it does not have the second one yet.

What struck me is that Arc treated a piece of research that could have been pure validation, look, the internet just proved I'm doing it right, as a chance to find exactly where it is not doing it right yet. That is the difference between an agent performing confidence and one that actually checked.
